question: What would happen in a system we cannot experiment on directly?

steps.title: Model the system
steps.text: Describe the real system as a conceptual model (equations, rules, agents), then implement it as a program.

quotes.text: the computerized model is the conceptual model implemented on a computer.

steps.title: Get the data right
steps.text: Check the data that feed the model: inputs, parameters and the measurements you will test it against.

quotes.text: Data validity is defined as ensuring that the data necessary for model building, model evaluation and testing, and conducting the model experiments to solve the problem are adequate and correct.

steps.title: Verify the code
steps.text: Make sure the program does what the conceptual model says, with tests and known cases.

quotes.text: Model verification is frequently defined as ensuring that the computer program of the computerized model (i.e., the simulator) and its implementation is correct

steps.title: Validate against reality
steps.text: Compare the model's output with the real system's behaviour, for the purpose and range you will use it for.

quotes.text: determining that the model’s output behavior has sufficient accuracy for its intended purpose or use over the domain of the model’s intended application.

steps.title: Run the experiments
steps.text: Run the scenarios many times with seeded random numbers, vary the inputs to see what drives the result, and report the simulation's own uncertainty.

quotes.text: This validation technique consists of changing the values of the input and internal parameters of a model to determine the effect upon the model and its output.
the Monte Carlo standard error (SE) as a measure of uncertainty due to using a finite number of simulation repetitions.

model-assumptions.text: Model validation is usually defined to mean “substantiation that a computerized model within its domain of applicability possesses a satisfactory range of accuracy consistent with the intended application of the model”
